lead: This unit explains how an operating system manages the main memory of a computer. After reading it, the student can answer exam questions on allocation, paging, virtual memory and related algorithms.
about: Unit 4 consists of nine chapters that build a complete picture of memory management. Chapter 4.1 introduces the basic strategies and address spaces. Chapter 4.2 adds swapping of whole processes. Chapter 4.3 studies contiguous allocation and fragmentation. Chapter 4.4 explains paging and the TLB. Chapter 4.5 describes page‑table structures. Chapter 4.6 covers segmentation. Chapter 4.7 expands to virtual memory, demand paging, page faults and copy‑on‑write. Chapter 4.8 compares FIFO, LRU and optimal page‑replacement algorithms. Chapter 4.9 finishes with frame allocation, working‑set ideas and thrashing detection. Each chapter uses short examples, a focused figure and a warning about common exam traps.

chapters.idea: Different strategies to allocate main memory and define a process address space.
chapters.depth: Cover fixed and variable partitions, paging, segmentation and virtual address vs physical address. Define logical address, physical address, base register, limit register. Mention that some syllabi call this "memory allocation strategies". Explain when each strategy is preferred.

figure.title: Memory allocation flow
figure.aria: Shows the steps from a process request to allocation and address translation.

chapters.example: Physical memory = 64 KB, page size = 16 KB, base register = 0x8000, logical address = 0x2A3F. Compute the physical address.
chapters.trap: Confusing logical address with physical address or forgetting to add the base.
chapters.leave: Detailed paging mechanisms are covered in later chapters.

chapters.idea: Swapping moves whole processes between RAM and disk.
chapters.depth: Define swap space, when swapping is invoked, overhead, and difference from paging. Some syllabi list this as "swap‑space management". Show a simple policy: swap out the longest idle process.

figure.aria: Sequence of actions when a process is swapped out and another is swapped in.

chapters.example: RAM = 16 MB, swap space = 32 MB, processes P1‑P4 each need 8 MB. After loading P1 and P2, which process is swapped out to load P3?
chapters.trap: Assuming swapping always reduces response time without considering I/O cost.
chapters.leave: Paging details are introduced in the next chapter.

chapters.idea: Contiguous allocation suffers from internal and external fragmentation.
chapters.depth: Explain fixed vs dynamic partitions, internal fragmentation (unused part of allocated block) and external fragmentation (holes between blocks). Describe first‑fit, best‑fit and worst‑fit algorithms and compaction. Some syllabi name this "contiguous memory allocation".

figure.title: Memory map
figure.aria: Shows memory blocks before and after allocation, highlighting holes.

chapters.example: Total memory = 100 KB. Requests arrive in order: 20 KB, 35 KB, 10 KB. Using first‑fit, show the layout and compute external fragmentation.
chapters.trap: Mixing up internal and external fragmentation in calculations.
chapters.leave: Non‑contiguous schemes such as paging are covered next.

chapters.idea: Paging divides memory into equal pages and uses a TLB for fast translation.
chapters.depth: Define page, frame, page table, TLB, hit ratio. Derive effective access time: EAT = h·(t_TLB + t_mem) + (1‑h)·(t_TLB + 2·t_mem). Some syllabi refer to this simply as "paging".

figure.title: Address translation path
figure.aria: Shows how a logical address passes through the TLB, page table and finally reaches RAM.

chapters.example: TLB hit ratio = 0.8, t_TLB = 1 ns, t_mem = 100 ns. Compute the effective access time.
chapters.trap: Forgetting the extra memory access when the TLB misses.
chapters.leave: Structure of the page table is examined in the next chapter.

chapters.idea: Page‑table structures organize entries for fast lookup.
chapters.depth: Cover single‑level, two‑level hierarchical and inverted page tables. List entry fields: present bit, frame number, protection bits, dirty bit. Show size calculation for a 32‑bit address with 4 KB pages. Some syllabi call this "structure of the page table".

figure.aria: Illustrates a two‑level page table hierarchy.

chapters.example: 32‑bit address, page size 4 KB. Two‑level table uses 10‑bit indexes for each level. Compute the number of entries in each level.
chapters.trap: Confusing the number of bits used for indexing with the total number of pages.

chapters.idea: Segmentation divides a process address space into logical segments.
chapters.depth: Define segment table, base‑limit pair, protection per segment, and segment fault. Mention external fragmentation still possible. Some syllabi list this as "segmentation". Briefly note segmented paging as a hybrid.

figure.title: Segment → page lookup
figure.aria: Shows the two‑step translation when segmentation is combined with paging.

chapters.example: Segment 2: base = 0x3000, limit = 0x2000. Logical address = 0x3500. Compute the physical address after segment check.
chapters.trap: Ignoring the limit check and producing an address outside the segment.
chapters.leave: Virtual memory and demand paging are covered in the next chapter.

chapters.idea: Virtual memory uses demand paging and copy‑on‑write to extend RAM with disk.
chapters.depth: Define virtual memory, demand paging, page‑fault handling steps, and copy‑on‑write (marked as advanced). Show effective access time formula with page‑fault rate. Some syllabi refer to this as "virtual memory" and "demand paging".

figure.aria: Sequence of messages when a page fault occurs and the required page is fetched from disk.

chapters.example: Memory access time = 100 ns, page‑fault service time = 8 ms, fault rate = 0.001. Compute the effective access time.
chapters.trap: Using the fault rate directly as a probability per instruction without accounting for the long service time.
chapters.leave: Specific replacement policies are examined in the next chapter.

chapters.idea: Page‑replacement algorithms decide which page to evict on a miss.
chapters.depth: Explain FIFO, LRU (stack implementation) and optimal (Belady) algorithms. Provide reference‑string examples and count page faults. Some syllabi list these three algorithms. Mention that optimal is theoretical only.

figure.title: Reference string simulation
figure.aria: Shows page‑fault counts for FIFO, LRU and Optimal on the same reference string.

chapters.example: Reference string: 1 2 3 4 1 2 5 1 2 3 4 5 with 3 frames. Compute page faults for FIFO, LRU and Optimal.
chapters.trap: Assuming LRU always yields fewer faults than FIFO without checking the reference pattern.
chapters.leave: Frame allocation and thrashing are discussed next.

chapters.idea: Frame allocation policies and thrashing detection keep the system responsive.
chapters.depth: Describe proportional allocation, global vs local replacement, working‑set model (advanced), and thrashing symptoms. Show how to detect thrashing by high page‑fault rate. Some syllabi call this "allocation of frames" and "thrashing".

figure.aria: Gantt chart showing frequent page faults for two processes that lead to thrashing.

chapters.example: Two processes each need 4 pages. Total frames = 6. Using proportional allocation, compute frames per process and show that both experience thrashing.
chapters.trap: Ignoring that global replacement can starve a process even when local allocation would not.
